lead: Hard and soft acids and bases (HSAB) is a rule for predicting which ions and molecules prefer each other. A hard acid or base is small, highly charged and holds its electrons tightly, so it is not easily polarised. A soft acid or base is large, lightly charged and easily polarised. Hard prefers hard, soft prefers soft. Chemists use this to choose precipitating agents, explain chelation, and select catalysts. Only a few universities teach HSAB as a named topic.
prereq: You need: 1.5 for ionic bonding and 1.6 for metal ions.

blocks.text: An acid is an electron-pair acceptor; a base is an electron-pair donor. In HSAB, hardness is about charge density, not pH. Charge density is charge divided by volume. A small ion with a high charge has high charge density. Its electron cloud is held tightly and resists distortion. Such an acid or base is hard. A large ion with a low charge has low charge density. Its outer electrons are loosely held and the cloud distorts easily. Such an acid or base is soft. Polarisability is the ease with which an electron cloud is distorted. High polarisability means soft; low polarisability means hard.

Hard acids include H<sup>+</sup>, Mg<sup>2+</sup> and Al<sup>3+</sup>. Hard bases include F<sup>−</sup>, OH<sup>−</sup>, H<sub>2</sub>O and NH<sub>3</sub>. Soft acids include Ag<sup>+</sup>, Hg<sup>2+</sup> and Cu<sup>+</sup>. Soft bases include I<sup>−</sup>, S<sup>2−</sup>, CN<sup>−</sup> and CO. Borderline acids such as Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Cu<sup>2+</sup> sit between the two groups. The rule is simple: hard–hard pairs form strong ionic or electrostatic bonds; soft–soft pairs form strong covalent bonds; hard–soft pairs are weaker.

blocks.where: q is the charge on the ion in coulombs; V is its volume in cubic metres.

blocks.text: Silver iodide, AgI, is far less soluble than silver fluoride, AgF, in water. HSAB explains the trend. Ag<sup>+</sup> is large and soft. I<sup>−</sup> is large and soft, so the Ag<sup>+</sup>–I<sup>−</sup> interaction has strong covalent character. F<sup>−</sup> is small and hard; it pairs poorly with soft Ag<sup>+</sup>. Therefore AgI is favoured and AgF is less favoured. This predicts precipitation: adding I<sup>−</sup> to Ag<sup>+</sup> gives AgI even when F<sup>−</sup> is present. The same logic explains why soft metal ions like Hg<sup>2+</sup> bind strongly to soft sulfur donors in proteins. Chelating ligands are chosen with matching hardness: a hard metal such as Al<sup>3+</sup> prefers hard O or F donors; a soft metal such as Hg<sup>2+</sup> prefers S donors. In catalysis, a soft metal surface binds soft reactants more strongly; a hard support binds hard groups. Do not use pH to classify hardness: HCl is a strong acid in water, but chloride is a borderline-to-soft base; the proton H<sup>+</sup> is hard.

examples.question: A mixture contains Ag<sup>+</sup> ions and both F<sup>−</sup> and I<sup>−</sup> at equal concentration. Using HSAB, predict which silver halide forms first, and explain why.
steps: Identify the acid: Ag<sup>+</sup> is large and has low charge density, so it is soft.
Identify the bases: F<sup>−</sup> is small with high charge density, so it is hard; I<sup>−</sup> is large and polarisable, so it is soft.
Match: soft Ag<sup>+</sup> with soft I<sup>−</sup> gives the stronger interaction; hard F<sup>−</sup> pairs poorly with soft Ag<sup>+</sup>.
Predict: AgI forms first and is less soluble; AgF remains more soluble.
examples.answer: AgI forms first because soft Ag<sup>+</sup> pairs with soft I<sup>−</sup>; AgF is less favoured because hard F<sup>−</sup> pairs poorly with soft Ag<sup>+</sup>.

traps: Hardness is not acid strength. HCl is a strong acid in water, but H<sup>+</sup> is hard and Cl<sup>−</sup> is borderline-to-soft; pH does not classify HSAB.
Size beats charge count: Li<sup>+</sup> is hard and Cs<sup>+</sup> is soft, even though both carry +1.
Cu<sup>2+</sup> is borderline; Cu<sup>+</sup> is soft. Do not treat all copper ions as one class.
Do not swap the bond descriptions: hard–hard is ionic or electrostatic; soft–soft is covalent.
A hard base does not always give an insoluble salt. Match the acid before predicting precipitation.

quiz.a: A hard acid is a small, highly charged electron-pair acceptor with low polarisability.
I<sup>−</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup>; CN<sup>−</sup> and CO are also soft bases.
I<sup>−</sup> is large, so its outer electrons are loosely held and its electron cloud is easily polarised.

quiz.q: Why does AgI form in preference to AgF?
quiz.a: Ag<sup>+</sup> is soft; I<sup>−</sup> is soft and F<sup>−</sup> is hard. The soft–soft AgI interaction is stronger than the hard–soft AgF interaction.

quiz.q: Predict whether Hg<sup>2+</sup> prefers F<sup>−</sup> or I<sup>−</sup>.
quiz.a: Hg<sup>2+</sup> is soft; I<sup>−</sup> is soft and F<sup>−</sup> is hard, so Hg<sup>2+</sup> prefers I<sup>−</sup>.

quiz.q: A catalyst binds CO strongly. Is the metal centre likely hard or soft? Explain.
quiz.a: CO is a soft base; a soft metal centre such as Pd<sup>2+</sup> or Ag<sup>+</sup> binds it strongly by soft–soft matching. A hard centre such as Al<sup>3+</sup> would bind CO poorly.

quiz.q: Why is pH not a valid HSAB scale?
quiz.a: pH measures H<sup>+</sup> activity in water. HSAB hardness depends on charge density and polarisability of the acid or base. A strong acid can contain a hard cation and a soft anion, so pH cannot classify both. Hardness is not acidity.

beyond: Not for the exam. HSAB is used in medicinal chemistry to design chelating drugs that remove toxic soft metals such as Hg<sup>2+</sup> and Pb<sup>2+</sup> from the body. In environmental chemistry, soft–soft binding explains why sulfide minerals trap heavy metal ions. Catalyst designers match a metal centre to a reactant. Search for 'Pearson HSAB principle', 'chelation therapy heavy metals' and 'soft metal catalysis'.
